item.title: 01 Introduction
item.description:
RĀJADHARMA

( GOVERNMENT AND STATECRAFT)

CHAPTER I

[[P1]][[Rajadharma|Rājadharma]] has been a subject of discussion in works on [[dharmasastra|dharmaśāstra]] from very ancient times. The Āp. Dh. S. II. 9.25.1 says [[“The|‘The]] general and special [[dharnus|dharmas]] of all varṇas have been explained: but now we shall declare the dharmas of a king in [[particular!|particular’.]] Āp. then states that the king should cause to be built a capital and a palace, the gates of which both should face the south; that the palace should be in the heart of the capital; that in front of the capital there was to be a hall called [[‘aman trana’|‘āmantraṇa’]] (hall of invitation); that to the south of the town there was to be an assembly house with doors on the north and south. Āp. requires that in the king’s realm no brāhmaṇa should suffer hunger, sickness, cold or heat; [[Ap.|Āp.]] gives regulations about the assembly house and about persons who were to be allowed to engage in gambling; he prescribes that [[the exercise in)|(the exercise in)]] arms, dancing, singing and music should not go on anywhere except in the houses of the king’s servants, that the king was to see that there was no danger from thieves in villages and forests, that the king should donate fields and money to brāhmaṇas according to their worth without detriment to his servants, that the king who meets death in recovering the property of [[brāh mapas|brāhmaṇas]] and other warlike persons who meet death in fighting for a similar worthy cause reap the merit of a sacrifice [[(i, e,| (i. e.]] reach heaven as reward); that the king should appoint in towns and [[Villages|villages]] officers and their subordinates, who are pure and [[truth ful,|truthful,]] for the protection of the subjects against thieves and who are to be made to make good what is stolen; that they are to collect lawful taxes for the king from the people except from learned brāhmaṇas, women of all castes, minors, students [[stay. ing|staying]] with teachers and ascetics fulfilling the rules of their order, [[sūdras|śūdras]] who do menial work for the higher castes (such as washing their feet), persons that are blind, deaf or dumb. [[Ap.|Āp.]] then lays down punishments for adultery and rape, for slander and defamation, for manslaughter, for theft and appropriation of another’s land, for breach of contract to cultivate the field of another, for a [[herdeman|herdsman]] leaving his herd or negligently allowing [[P2]]it to perish. He states that if the king does not punish the guilty he incurs sin, that in disputes judges should be men of learning, clever and fulfilling their duties, that witnesses were to tell the truth and were to be punished if they be untruthful. It will be noticed how [[Ap.|Āp.]] briefly covers the whole field of [[rājam dharma.|rājadharma.]] In the [[Sāntiparva|Śāntiparva]] of the Mahābhārata rājadharma is dealt with at great length in chapters 56-130 and to some extent in [[131-17%.|131-172.]] The [[Manusmrti|Manusmṛti]] also states at the beginning of chap. VII (1) that it will expound rājadharmas. That great literary activity on the science and art of government went on for many centuries before the Christian era follows from several considerations. The Anuśāsanaparva (chap. 39.8) speaks of the śāstras composed by [[Bphaspati|Bṛhaspati]] and [[Usanas.|Uśanas.]] The [[Santi parva|Śāntiparva]] (58.1-3) names as expounders of [[rājaśūstra|rājaśāstra]] [[Bphaspati|Bṛhaspati]], Bharadvāja, Gauraśiras, Kāvya, Mahendra, Manu [[Pracetasa|Prācetasa]] and [[Visalākṣa.|Viśālākṣa.]] [[Sāntiparva|Śāntiparva]] (102.31-32) opposes the view of Śambara to that of [[acāryas|ācāryas]]1. The Arthaśāstra of [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] mentions five schools (viz. those of the Mānavas, the Bārhaspatyas, the [[Ausa nasas,|Auśanasas,]] the [[Pārāsaras|Pārāśaras]] and the [[Ambhiyas|Āmbhiyas]]), seven individual [[tea chers|teachers]] (V. 5, and I. 8) only once (viz. [[Bāhudantiputra|Bāhudantīputra]], [[Dirgha|Dīrgha]] Cārāyaṇa, [[Ghotamukha|Ghoṭamukha]], [[Kaṇinka|Kaṇiṅka]] Bhāradvāja, Kātyāyana, [[Kin jalka|Kiñjalka]], [[Pigunaputra,)|Piśunaputra,)]] and several times mentions the views of Bhāradvāja, Kauṇapadanta, Parāśara, [[Pisuna|Piśuna]], Vātavyādhi, Viśālākṣa. [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] also cites at least 53 times the views of [[acāryas|ācāryas]], almost in every case for dissent. [[Sānti|Śānti]] 103.44 refers to a [[Bhāsya|Bhāṣya]] on [[rājasāstra.|rājaśāstra.]] Is it possible to see in this a reference to one out of the [[bhāsyakāras|bhāṣyakāras]] indicated in the verse appended at the end of the [[Kauṭiliya|Kauṭilīya]] or to the Kauṭilīya itself? Another fact indicative of the [[systematiza tion|systematization]] of the science of government is that in the Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa, Manu and [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] ideas expressed by numbers had already been stereotyped long before those works were written viz. such as [[saptāóga|saptāṅga]] rājya (State with seven constituent [[elements ),|elements),]] [[ṣadguṇya|ṣāḍguṇya]] (the six ways of policy viz. alliance, declaration of war &c.), three śaktis, the four upāyas (sāma, [[dana|dāna]], bheda, [[danda|daṇḍa]]), [[astavarga,|aṣṭavarga,]] and pañcavarga (Manu VII. 155), the 18 and 15 [[tirthas|tīrthas]] (Sabhāparva 5.38)2. For detailed information [[P3]]about the Rājaśāstras of [[Bșhaspati|Bṛhaspati]], Uśanas, Bhāradvāja culled from the [[Mahabharata|Mahābhārata]] and other ancient works vide my paper on them in the Journal of the University of Bombay, vol. XI part 2 pp. 73-83, 1942.

item.title: 02 Seven Aṅgas of Rājya
item.description:
CHAPTER II.

SEVEN [[ANGAS|AṄGAS]] OF [[RAJYA|RĀJYA]]

[[P17]]According to almost all of our authorities a state ([[rūjya|rājya]]) is constituted by seven elements 1 viz. svāmin (ruler or sovereign), [[amūtya|amātya]] (minister), janapada or [[rāṣtra|rāṣṭra]] (the territory of the State and its people), durga (fortified city or capital), kośa ([[accumula ted|accumulated]] wealth in the ruler’s treasury), [[dandu|daṇḍa]] (army), mitra (friends or allies). These seven are called [[angas|aṅgas]] or [[praktis|prakṛtis]]. The word [[praksti|prakṛti]] in works on politics is also used for the constituents of a circle of states (of a [[mandala|maṇḍala]]). Vide Manu VII. 156 and [[Kau tilya|Kauṭilya]] (VI. 2). The word also means ministers as in [[Sukranitisāra|Śukranītisāra]] II. 70-73 and ‘subjects’ in Khāravela’s Inscription (E. I. vol. 20 [[p.79 1. 4|p. 79 l. 4]]), Nārada ([[prakirnaka|prakīrṇaka]] 5), [[Raghuvamsa|Raghuvaṁśa]] VIII. 18. The order in which these are arranged and their names vary a good deal. The quotations given below will indicate how the order differs. The sequence is important for the reason that some of our authorities expressly state that when calamities [[be fall|befall]] or deterioration sets in each of the seven elements, those that befall each preceding one are more serious for the State than those of each succeeding one ([[ Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] VIII. 1, Manu IX. 295). For janapada sometimes the word jana or [[rāṣtra|rāṣṭra]] is used, for [[* danda’|‘daṇḍa’]] the word ‘bala’ and the word ‘pura’ for ‘durga’. The [[Aśramavāsiparva|Āśramavāsiparva]] (5. 8) speaks of eight [[angas|aṅgas]] of rājya. [[Accord ing|According]] to Sumantu quoted by the [[Sarasvativilāsa|Sarasvatīvilāsa]] (p. 46) [[danda|daṇḍa]] means “punishment bodily or monetary” and [[’ army|‘army’]] is included under ‘kośa’. Sumantu says that [[th esvūmin|the svāmin]] has to be preserved by himself, the ministers by showing them proper respect, the people by keeping them contented, the fortified capital by abundance of wealth and grain, the kośa by proper expenditure, [[danda|daṇḍa]] [[P18]]by following one’s dharma, friends by truthfulness. The authorities are agreed that the ruler is the most important or the first of the seven. [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] puts the matter very forcibly and realistically when he states that the briefest exposition of the elements of rājya is to say that the king is the State 2. This is really not the same doctrine as that emphasized by Louis XIV of France when he said ‘L’Etat c’est moi’. [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] makes his position clear (in [[VIII, 1|VIII. 1]]) by saying that it is the king who appoints ministers and servants and superintendents, who takes measures of relief against calamities befalling the other [[prakstis|prakṛtis]] and measures of prosperity, that it is he who appoints other ministers when those already appointed are under calamities, that if the ruler is prosperous he transmits prosperity to his [[prakstis|prakṛtis]], that the [[prakstis|prakṛtis]] bear that character which the king has and that hence the ruler occupies the position of a permanent, never-exhausted centre of power. The [[Sukranitisāra|Śukranītisāra]] [[II4|II. 4]] remarks that if the king begins to act at his sweet will, it leads to calamities, to loss of ministers and of the kingdom. The [[Sukranitisāra|Śukranītisāra]] (I. 61-62) compares the seven [[angās|aṅgas]] of rājya to the organs of the body viz., the king is the head, the ministers are the eyes, ally the ear, treasury the mouth, the army the mind, capital and [[rāṣtra|rāṣṭra]] are hands and feet. It is emphasized by Kām. (IV. 1-2) that each of the seven elements is complementary to the others, that if the state is defective even in one out of the seven elements it does not pull well. [[thel Sāntiparva|In the Śāntiparva]] it is stated that it is not possible to say categorically that any one of the seven excels the others in merit, but that at different times a different element assumes importance over others, since that particular element is in the particular circumstances capable of accomplishing the purpose in hand. This shows that Manu and the Mahābhārata held that there was an organic unity in the several elements of rājya. All must work harmoniously towards one ideal or end. Manu (IX. 296–297) says this by means of a simile ‘Just as among the three staves tied together (by a rope of cow’s hair) used by a sannyāsin no particular staff is superior (to the others), so among [[P19]]the seven elements of the state no particular one can be said to excel the others, since each of them has a particular excellence of its own; a particular element is pre-eminent in some particular matter and therefore the superiority of one to the others when expressed (as e. g. in Manu IX. 295) is to be [[confinod|confined]] to that matter alone.’ Manu here emphasizes the harmonious working or unity of the seven elements though they are diverse in their individual characters. The analysis of the elements and nature of the State led ancient Indian writers to hold that a mere conglomeration of people did not by itself constitute a State, but that for a State there must be people who live within certain definite geographical limits ([[rāstra|rāṣṭra]]), they must be bound by the bond to render allegiance to a ruler ([[svāmi|svāmī]]), [[inust have|must have]] a certain system of government (amātya), must have a regulated economic system, a force for defence and international relationships. That is, the most essential elements of a state are (1) a sovereign, (2) a system of government, (3) a definite territory and (4) [[&|a]] population of some size. These four were known even to the most ancient sūtras. Vide Gaut. XI. 1 ([[rāja|rājā]]), [[Ap.|Āp.]] II. 6. 25. 10 (amātya), [[Ap.|Āp.]] II. 10. 25. 11, [[II, 10, 26. 4|II. 10. 26. 4]] ([[visaya|viṣaya]], nagara, grāma), [[Gaut|Gaut.]] XI. 5-8 (prajā).

item.title: 03 Duties of the Ruler
item.description:
CHAPTER III

DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF

THE RULER.

[[P56]]All works are agreed that the first and foremost duty of the king is the protection of subjects. [[Sāntiparva|Śāntiparva]] (68. 1-4) notes that all the seven expounders of polity ([[rājaśāstraprane tāraḥ|rājaśāstrapraṇetāraḥ]]) named by it extol protection as the highest dharma of the king. Manu VII. 144 states that the protection of subjects is the highest dharma and Kālidāsa in [[Raghuvamsa|Raghuvaṁśa]] 14.67 alludes to this dictum of Manu. Protection consists in punishing internal aggression (such as by thieves and robbers and by persons who invade a man’s rights) and in meeting external1 aggression. Vide quotation from [[Bphaspati|Bṛhaspati]] below. Gautama (X. 7-8) prescribes that the special responsibility of the king is to protect all beings, to award just punishment and that he has to protect the several varṇas and [[aśramas|āśramas]] according to the rules of śāstra and to bring them round to the path of their proper duties when they swerve from it (XI. 9-10). [[Vasiṣtha|Vasiṣṭha]] (19. 1-2) states that the wise say that protection is a life-long sattra in which he has to give up fear and softness of heart. Vas. 19. 7-8 and Viṣṇu Dh. S. III. 2-3 are similar to Gaut. XI. 9-10. The [[Sāntiparva|Śāntiparva]] (23.15) repeats a [[gātha|gāthā]] of [[Bphaspati.|Bṛhaspati ‘]]As a snake [[gwallows|swallows]] mice lying in holes, so the earth swallows these two viz. a king who does not fight (an invader) and a [[brāhmana|brāhmaṇa]] who does not go on a journey (for acquiring knowledge from famous teachers)’.2 Manu IX. 306 states that the king protecting his subjects according to the śāstra and meting out punishment to those who deserve it performs every day sacrifices in which the fees are one hundred thousand cows (i.e. he secures the spiritual reward of very solemn sacrifices). Yāj. I. 335 is to the same effect. [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] also lays emphasis on the duty to keep the varṇas and āśramas to their duties ‘Therefore the

item.title: 04 Ministers
item.description:
CHAPTER IV

MINISTERS

[[P104]][[Amatya -The|Amātya—The]] second of the seven elements of rājya is the [[amālya|amātya]], which word may be translated as ‘minister.’ There are three words that are interchangeable though sometimes [[dis tinguished|distinguished]], viz. [[amõtya|amātya]], saciva and mantrin, the first being the oldest of the three. A Kārikā on Pāṇini (IV. 2. 104) teaches the formation of the word with the affix tyap (tya) from [[ama|amā]] meaning [[near|‘near]] or with’ [[( vide|(vide]] Mahābhāṣya, vol. II. p. 292). In [[Rg.|Ṛg.]] IV. 4. 11 there is the germ of this word ‘O [[Agnil|Agni!]] Go like a king riding an elephant, accompanied by his ministers[[’ .|’]] Yāska (in Nirukta VI. [[12 )|12)]] explains [[’ amayān ‘|‘amavān’]] as [[‘amātya vān,’|‘amātyavān,’]] though two more explanations of the word are offered by him. The word [[amatya|amātya]] itself occurs in [[Rg.|Ṛg.]] VII. 15. 3, but there it is an adjective and means ‘our own’ or [[’ abiding|‘abiding]] in our [[house ‘.|house’.]] In some of the sūtras like the Baudhāyana[[pitf-medhasūtra|pitṛ-medhasūtra]] (I. [[A.|4.]] 13, I. 12. [[7 )|7)]] the word amātya is used in the sense of ’near male relations in the house’. Vide H. [[Dh,|Dh.]] vol. II. p. 588 n. 1375. The word [[’ amātya’|‘amātya’]] occurs in the sense of minister in [[Ap. Dh. 8.|Āp. Dh. S.]] II. 10. 25. 10 [[The|‘The]] king should not live better or more luxuriously than his gurus [[( elders)|(elders)]] and his ministers ([[gurūn amātyānsca nātijivet|gurūn-amātyāṁśca nātijīvet]])’. The word [[‘gaciva’|‘saciva’]] occurs in the Ait. Br. [[( XII. 9)|(XII. 9)]] where it is said that Indra considered the Maruts as his ‘sacivas’ (helpers or comrades). The necessity of [[amatyas|amātyas]] or sacivas is stated in graphic language by several writers. [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] (I. 7 last [[verse )|verse)]] says ‘kingship is possible only with [[( the aid of)|(the aid of)]] assistants, a single wheel cannot work [[( a chariot );|(a chariot);]] therefore the king should appoint ministers and listen to their opinions[[’ .|’]] Manu [[( VII. 55 = Sukra II. 1)|(VII. 55 = Śukra II. 1)]] says [[it|‘it]] is difficult for a person single-handed to accomplish even an easy [[task ;|task;]] how can government particularly, which has great good as its aim, be accomplished without helpers’? The Matsya-purāṇa [[( 215. 2 )|(215. 2)]] prescribes [[the|‘the]] king, while his head is still wet with the waters of coronation, if he wants to supervise his State, should choose his helpers, as in the latter the kingdom secures stability[[’ .|’]] Matsya 215. 3 is the same as Manu VII. 55. Vide [[P105]]Viṣṇudharmottara II. 24. 2-3 which are the same as Matsya 215. 2-3; also [[śānti|Śānti]] 106. 11 and [[Rājanttiprakāśa|Rājanītiprakāśa]] p. 174. From Arthaśāstra I. [[."|7]] and 8, Manu [[VII,|VII.]] 54 and 60, Kām. IV. 25, 27, [[XIII,|XIII.]] 24 and 64 it appears that they use the words saciva and amātya as synonyms. Rudradāman in his [[Junāgadh|Junāgaḍh]] Inscription2 (E. I. vol. VIII. p. 36 at p. [[44 )|44)]] states that his great enterprise to repair the [[Sudarsana|Sudarśana]] lake was disapproved of by his advisory (mati-saciva) and executive councillors (karma[[-saciva| saciva]]) who were all endowed with the qualities required in amātyas and yet who were averse to the project and had no enthusiasm for it, since the breach to be repaired was very great. Here sacivas are divided into two sorts, those who give advice and those who execute the business decided upon and the word [[baciva|saciva]] seems to be a synonym of amātya. Amara3 states that the amātya who is a [[dhisaciva|dhīsaciva]] (i. e. matisaciva) is called a mantrin, while amātyas other than the mantrin are called karmasacivas. These distinctions are often not observed. Sumantra is called amātya in Rāmāyaṇa I. 7. 3 and the best of mantrins in I. 8. 4. In [[Ayodhya|Ayodhyā]] 112. 17 [[amatya|amātya]] and mantrin seem to be distinguished. From [[Kaut.|Kauṭ.]] I. 8 (last [[verse )|verse)]] [[’ Having|‘Having]] divided the spheres of their powers and having taken into consideration the time and place and the work they have to do, all these persons should be appointed as ministers [[( amātyas ),|(amātyas),]] but not as mantrins,’ it follows that mantrins were regarded by [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] as of a higher grade than amātyas in general. The R. N. P. p. 178 says that the amātyas are also styled mantrins. [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] states (I. [[10 )|10)]] how amātyas are to be tested by upadhās i. e. by means of tempting them as regards each of [[dlurnu|dharma]], artha, [[kama|kāma]], and bhaya (fear) and to be employed if found honest after any one of the four tests, while mantrins were to be [[appoint ed|appointed]] only if their integrity and loyalty were proved by all the tests combined. Upadhā4 is defined by the [[Nitivākyāmrta|Nītivākyāmṛta]] p. 111 as ’testing the mind of a person as regards dharma, artha, [[kama|kāma]] and bhaya by various devices’ [[( employed|(employed]] by secret agents). Kāt. (4-[[5 )|5)]] quoted by R. N. P. p. 136 states that the minds of kings always go astray on the (slightest) cause by [[P106]]reason of the fact that they possess great valour, knowledge, wealth and particularly the fact that they possess absolute power; therefore brāhmaṇas should always enlighten the mind of the king as to the duties of a king.

item.title: 05 Rāṣṭra
item.description:
CHAPTER V

[[RĀSTRA|RĀṢṬRA]] (THE TERRITORY OF A STATE)

[[P132]]The word ‘[[rāstra|rāṣṭra]]’ occurs even in the [[Rgveda|Ṛgveda]] (IV. 42.1, ‘[[mania|mama]] dvitā [[rāstram|rāṣṭraṁ]] kṣatriyasya’)—‘mine is the kingdom on both sides (or in both spheres)’ says king Trasadasyu. In [[Rg.|Ṛg.]] VII. [[34,11|34.11]] [[Varuna|Varuṇa]] is praised as the Lord of [[rāṣtras|rāṣṭras]] ([[rājā rāṣtrāṇām &c.).|rājā rāṣṭrāṇāṁ &c.).]] In [[Rg.|Ṛg.]] VII. 84.2 and X. 109. 3 the word [[rāstra|rāṣṭra]] occurs. In a very famous benedictory 1 passage of the Tai. S. VII. 5. 18. [[10 =|1( =]] Vāj. S. [[22.22 )|22.22)]] one of the blessings invoked is ‘may the king in this kingdom become brave, a skilled archer, and a great [[warrior’, Vide Tai, Br. III. 8. 13 for explanation of the Tai, S. passage.|warrior’. Vide Tai. Br. III. 8. 13 for explanation of the Tai. S. passage.]] In the Atharvaveda XII. 1. 8 and 10 the earth is called mother and invoked to impart to the [[rāṣtra|rāṣṭra]] strength and brilliance (or [[energy ).|energy).]] Kām. VI. 3 says 2 that since all the elements of the State spring from the territory of the State, the king should raise up his territory with all his efforts. The Agnipurāṇa [[239, 2|239. 2]] holds that [[rāṣtra|rāṣṭra]] is the most important of all elements of the State. Manu VII. 69 prescribes that a king should make his home in a country that is not water-logged (i. e. is dry and not [[moist ), 176|moist),]]3 is rich in crops, inhabited mostly by [[Aryas|Āryas]] (or well-conducted [[people ),|people),]] not disturbed (by epidemics [[&c. ),|&c.),]] that is charming (owing to trees, flowers and [[fruits ),|fruits),]] the chiefs in which have submitted to him and in which livelihood can be had easily. Yāj. I. 321 and Viṣṇudharmasūtra III. 4-5 are to the same [[.effect.|effect.]] Kām. (IV. [[50-56 )|50-56)]] remarks [[the|‘the]] territory of [[P133]]the king depends for its prosperity on the qualities of the soil, the prosperity of the territory tends to the prosperity of the king; therefore a king should choose for the sake of his prosperity land possessing good qualities. That land is [[prefer red|preferred]] for the sake of prosperity that is endowed with various crops and minerals, is full of merchandise, mines and various substances, that is favourable to cattle-rearing, that abounds in water, is inhabited by well-conducted people, is charming, has forests and elephants, has facilities of water and road transport and does not depend upon rain-water [[only.’ 177|only.’]]4 Land that is full of gravel and stones, full of forests always infested with thieves, that is waterless, full of thorny bushes and snakes is not fit for choosing as a [[rūśtra.|rāṣṭra.]] A country is to be preferred that yields livelihood easily, is possessed of the qualities of good land (cited above), is full of water, that has hills in it, that consists mostly of [[sūdras,|śūdras,]] artisans and merchants, the husbandmen in which undertake great projects, that is loyal [[(to the king )|(to the king)]] and averse to the king’s enemy, that can put up with troubles and taxes, that is large in extent, full of people from various countries, that follows the right path, that possesses plenty of cattle and wealth, the principal men in which are not foolish nor vicious. These requirements show that the country must be prosperous, well-stocked with the necessaries of life and well suited to defence. There is also some difference of opinion among the [[smrti|smṛti]] writers about the composition of the population. Manu VII. 69 requires that the kingdom should consist mostly of [[aryas|āryas]] (āryaprāya), while Viṣṇu Dh. S. III. 5 holds that a country should be peopled mostly by vaiśyas and [[sūdras.|śūdras.]] In another place (VIII. 22) Manu says that that country in which [[sūdras|śūdras]] abound, which is full of atheists and void of dvijas is overwhelmed by disease and famine and perishes. Similar provisions are found in the [[Matsyapurana|Matsyapurāṇa]] 217. 1-5, Viṣṇudharmottara II. 26. 1-5, [[Mānasol lasa|Mānasollāsa]] (II. 3. verses 151-153), [[Nitivākyāmsta|Nītivākyāmṛta]] (Janapadasamuddeśa p. 191 which defines [[rāṣtra,|rāṣṭra,]] viṣaya, deśa, janapada &c.). The Matsyapurāṇa 217. 5 and Viṣṇudharmottara II. [[26.5, (pvainvidhain ynthālābham rajā viṣny amāriset)|26. 5, (evaṁvidhaṁ yathālābhaṁ rājā viṣayamāvaset)]] point out that [[P134]][[overy|every]] [[rāṣtra|rāṣṭra]] cannot be expected to possess all the qualities mentioned by them and that the king must do the best with such qualities as his country possesses. [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] II. 1 [[advises 178|advises]]5 the king to found a district of villages either on old sites or on new ones by inducing people from other countries to immigrate or by causing thickly populated parts of his own country to send its overflowing population and to see that each village consists of not less than one hundred families nor more than five hundred, is peopled mostly by śūdra cultivators, has an extent of one [[krosa|krośa]] or two and is capable of offering help to its neighbours.

item.title: 06 Durgā
item.description:
[[P178]] CHAPTER VI

DURGA ( FORT OR CAPITAL)

Manu [[IX,|IX.]] 294 places the capital (pura) even before [[rastra|rāṣṭra]]. Medhātithi (on IX. 295 ) and Kullūka explain that the loss of the capital is a more serious danger than even the loss of some territory, because if the capital, which possesses all the stocks of food, in which are centred the principal elements and the army, is saved, then it is possible to retrieve even lost territory and to protect the country. It is as it were the pivot of the whole machinery of government. Other writers (and even Manu in VII. 69-70) place the capital or fort after the [[rastra|rāṣṭra]]. It is probably due to the geographical situation in North India and the nature of the fighting in ancient times that made the [[capi tal|capital]] and forts of great importance in the several elements of the State. The capital mirrored the prosperity of the country and if properly walled also provided security. Yāj. I. 321 says that forts are meant for the safety of the king, the people and the treasury (janakośātmaguptaye). The reason for the construction of forts is well put by Manu VII. 74 viz. that a single archer under the shelter of the fort-wall can fight a hundred of the enemy and a hundred can fight ten thousand. The Pañcatantra (I. 229 and II. 14 ) has a similar verse. [[Bphaspati|Bṛhaspati]] quoted by the Rājanītiprakāśa1 p. 202 states that the king should [[con struct|construct]] a fort with walls and a gate for the protection of himself, his wives, the people and the ( wealth ) collected by him. [[Kaut.|Kauṭ.]] (II. 3 and 4) deals at length with the construction of durgas and the laying out of the capital in one of them. He says that in the four quarters of the boundaries of the kingdom forts should be built for offering resistance (to the enemy) on ground naturally fitted for the purpose. He speaks of four kinds of forts viz. ‘audaka’ (water-protected, which is on an island [[burrounded|surrounded]] by water or on a plain surrounded by low ground), pārvata (mountain one, such as a rocky hill or a cave ), [[dhūnvana|dhānvana]] (desert fort, on a waterless tract full of thickets or waste land ), a forest fort full of wagtails and water and [[P179]] thickets of reed. He says that the first two are suited for the protection of populous places and the last two for the protection of foresters. [[Vayu 8. 108 •|Vāyu 8. 108]] refers to four kinds of durgas. Manu VII. 70, [[Sānti|Śānti]] 56. 35 and 86. 4-5, Viṣṇudharmasūtra III. 6, Matsya 217. 6-7, Agnipurāṇa 222. 4-5, [[Viṣṇudhar mottara|Viṣṇudharmottara]] II. 26. 6-9, III. 323. 16-21, [[Sukra|Śukra]] IV. 6 speak of six kinds of forts viz. dhanvadurga ( which is waterless five yojanas round a raised plain), [[mahidurga|mahīdurga]] (a land fort, which is surrounded by a wall built of stones or burnt bricks, that is at least twelve feet high and twice as high as it is broad), jaladurga ( water fort, surrounded on all sides by deep water), [[vārksa|vārkṣa]] durga (fort that is surrounded for one yojana on all sides with thorny and tall trees and thorny creepers and bushes), nṛdurga (fort that is guarded by a numerous army of four sections on all sides ), giridurga (mountain fortress, difficult to climb and with only one narrow access). Manu VII. 71 says that the mountain fortress is the best of all, while [[śānti|Śānti]] 56. 35 states that [[nrdurga|nṛdurga]] is the most difficult to conquer. The Mānasollāsa (II. 5 p. 78) speaks of nine kinds of durgas (adding those built with stones, bricks and mud). The [[Parasurama- pratāpa|Paraśurāma-pratāpa]] enumerates eight kinds of durgas ([[Rāja vallabhakānda|Rāja-vallabhakāṇḍa]], folio 1) and states that the wall of a fort may be of stones or of baked bricks or of mud. Manu VII. [[75|75,]] Sabhā 5. 36 ( =Ayodhyā [[100,|100.]] 53), Matsya 217. 8, Kām. [[IV,|IV.]] 60, [[Mānasollasa|Mānasollāsa]] III. 5 (verses 550-555), [[Sukra IV,|Śukra IV.]] 6. 12-13, [[Vigpu’ dharmottara|Viṣṇudharmottara]] II. 26. 20-88 prescribe that forts should possess plenty of arms, grain, drugs and other materials, wealth, horses, elephants, beasts of burden, [[brahmaṇas|brāhmaṇas]], artisans, machines (called [[Sataghnis|Śataghnīs]] acc. to Matsya, that kill a hundred), water and fodder. The [[Nitivākyāmṛta|Nītivākyāmṛta]] ( [[durga-samuddesa|durga-samuddeśa]] p. 199) says that there must be means of leaving it secretly, otherwise it will be a prison and that no one should be allowed to enter it or leave it without a pass or without being searched. [[Kaut.|Kauṭ.]] ( II. 3) gives detailed instructions for the construction of fort walls, towers, ditches, pillars, lotus ponds and buildings inside the fort, which are all passed over for want of space. Vide the [[Rājadharmakānda|Rājadharmakāṇḍa]] pp. 28-36 and the Rājadharmakaustubha pp. 115-117 for numerous quotations from the Dhanurveda of [[Uganas|Uśanas]], the Mahābhārata, the Matsya, the Viṣṇudharmottara and other works on [[durya|durga]].

item.title: 07 Kośa
item.description:
[[P184]] CHAPTER VII

KOSA (TREASURY OR FINANCE)

[[Kaut|Kauṭ.]] (II. 1) states that a king whose treasury is depleted preys upon the citizens and the rural population and (II. 8) very1 rightly remarks that all undertakings depend upon kośa (financial position of the king), therefore the king must pay the first attention to kośa. Gautama (as cited by [[8.|S.]] V. p. 46 ) holds that kośa is the basis or support of the other six elements of the State. The [[Sāntiparva|Śāntiparva]] 119. 16 calls upon the king to guard his finances with great effort, since kings depend upon kośa, which tends to the prosperity ( of the kingdom). Kām. XIII. 33 states that it is on the lips of all that the king is dependent on [[koga|kośa]]. [[Sānti|Śānti]] 133 contains a eulogy of kośa. The Viṣṇudharmottara II. [[61,|61.]] 17 says that kośa is the root of the tree of State. The two great pillars of the Indian States in ancient India were the revenue and the army. Manu VII. 65 says that kośa and the government of the realm depend on the king i. e. they should be the personal concern of the king. Yāj. (I. 327-328) recommends that the king should personally look into the income and expenditure every day and keep in his treasury buildings whatever is brought by those who are appointed to bring gold and wealth. Kām. [[V.77|V. 77]] and [[Sukra|Śukra]] I. 276-278 say the same. The [[Rājataran gini|Rājātaraṅgiṇī]] (VII. 507-508) tells us that king [[Kalasa|Kalaśa]] of Kashmir (1063–1089 A. D.) kept accounts like a merchant, closely watched income and expenditure and had a clerk by his side with chalk and bhūrja ( birch leaf) to write upon. The principal means of filling the treasury is taxation. It is therefore [[neces sary|necessary]] to consider first the principles of taxation as evolved by our writers. The first principle was that the king could not levy, according to the [[smrtis,|smṛtis,]] taxes at his pleasure or sweet will, that the rates of taxes which the king was entitled to [[lovy|levy]] were fixed by the [[smrtis|smṛtis]] and varied only according to the

item.title: 08 Bala
item.description:
[[P200]] CHAPTER VIII

BALA (THE ARMY).

Bala is also called [[danda|daṇḍa]] in [[Kaut|Kauṭ.]] and elsewhere. [[Accord ing|According]] to Sumantu [[dapda|daṇḍa]] means ‘punishment, corporal or monetary’ and the army with its four arms is included by Sumantu under kośa ( acc. to [[$. V.|S. V.]] p. 46).1 In the [[Rgveda|Ṛgveda]] we have frequent references to armies, weapons, battles &c. The word [[senāni|senānī]] occurs in [[Rg.|Ṛg.]] X. 84. 2 where Manyu ( martial Fury ) is invoked to be the Commander.2 [[Rg.|Ṛg.]] VI. 75 is full of references to bows, arrows, armour, bow-strings, quiver, charioteer, horses, chariots &c. Kām. ( XIII. 34–37 ) states that the king possessed of a sound financial position increases his depleted army, supports his own subjects and is depended upon even by his enemies. All the following result from the possession of a (powerful ) army viz. increase of the wealth of one’s friends and enemies and of the ( king’s) territories, prompt attainment of objects that seemed distant, protection of what is already [[secur ed|secured]], destruction of the armies of the enemy, the keeping together of one’s army. Most authorities agree in saying that troops are of six kinds viz. maula (hereditary ), [[bhrta|bhṛta]] or bhṛtaka or [[bhitya|bhṛtya]] (hired troops ), [[śreni|śreṇi]] (guild troops ), mitra ( troops of an ally or friendly power or feudatories ), amitra ( troops that once belonged to the enemy ), [[atavi|aṭavi]] or ātavika (wild tribes as troops). Vide [[Kaut. 242|Kauṭ.]]3 IX. [[%|2]] (first sentence ), Kām. XVIII. 4, Agnipurāṇa 242. 1–2, Mānasollāsa ( II. 6, [[verge|verse]] 556 p. 76). The first three works say that each earlier variety of troops is superior to each later one. Maula troops corresponded to the modern standing army, since [[Kaut.|Kauṭ.]] (IX. 2) prefers them on the ground that they depend on the king for maintenance and are being constantly drilled. They most probably consisted of persons who and whose ancestors got tax-free lands in lieu of military service. The [[Sabba parva 5, 63|Sabhāparva 5. 63]] appears to refer to four kinds ( omitting [[śreni|śreṇi]] and amitra ) and [[Yuddhakanda|Yuddhakāṇḍa]] 17. 24 refers to five ( omitting [[śrepi|śreṇi]]).

item.title: 09 Mitra
item.description:
[[P216]]CHAPTER IX

SUHṚT OR MITRA (ALLY OR FRIEND).

Manu inculcates the necessity of making friends in VII. 208 and cites the qualities of a good friend ([[for.|for]] a king) ‘a king does not prosper by the acquisition of gold and land so much as by securing a firm friend who would be powerful in future, though he may be of depleted resources at the time. That friend, though a weak one, is commended, who is righteous, grateful, whose subjects (or ministers) are contented, who is attached and who pursues (to the end) work undertaken’. According to Manu VII. 206 land, gold and ally are the three fruits of royal endeavour or policy. Yāj I. 352 is similar to Manu VII. 208. In VII. 9 [[Kautilya|Kauṭilya]] in opposition to the above holds that the acquisition of land is better than that of gold and friend and the acquisition of gold is superior to that of a friend1. The [[Mahā. bharata|Mahābhārata]] ([[Santi|Śānti]] 138.110) states ’no one is the friend or enemy of any one else; friends or enemies are made by wealth (or objects pursued by a person)’:[[285|’]]2 Kām. VIII. 52 says the same. [[Sukra.|Śukra.]] (IV. 1.[[8-10| 8-10)]] opines ‘in the case of a brave, energetic, strong and politic king all others, though outwardly friendly, secretly cherish enmity to [[bim|him]] and only wait for (the proper) time to strike ). There is no wonder in this. Are they not themselves greedy of conquering territories? A king has no friend and he is the friend of none’. [[Sānti|Śānti]] (80. 3) says3 that a friend is of four kinds, one who has the same goal, one who comes for [[protec tion|protection]] or security, one who is naturally [[go|so]] and one who is [[acqui. red|acquired]]. [[Karnaparva|Karṇaparva]] 88. 28 gives the four kinds somewhat [[diffe rently|differently]] viz. natural (sahaja), acquired by conciliatory words, [[P217]] won by wealth and one drawn by one’s prowess. Kām. (IV. 74) says that a mitra is of four kinds viz. by birth (such as one’s father’s father, mother &c.), made by relationship (i. e. marriage), hereditary (one’s father’s friend), one who is saved from calamities.4 According to Kām. ([[IV.75-76|IV. 75-76]]) the qualities of a friendly king are purity (of heart), liberality, bravery, sharing happiness and sorrow, affection, vigilance (to carry out one’s friend’s object), truth; and briefly the characteristic of a true friend is devotion to the objects desired by his friend. The purpose for which [[&|a]] friend is made is to secure one of the three [[purusārthas|puruṣārthas]], dharma, artha and kāma (Kām. IV. 72).

item.title: 10 Purpose of the Study of Rājadharma
item.description:
[[P235]] CHAPTER X

PURPOSE OF THE STUDY OF RĀJADHARMA AND THE ENDS OF THE STATE

In the preceding pages an attempt has been made to present a picture of the theory and practice of Government and [[state craft|state-craft]] as delineated by ancient and medieval Indian writers on dharmaśāstra and arthaśāstra. One feature that would strike any reader is the religious colouring with which all theories and ideals are suffused. Another is that the ideal set before rulers and their officers is a highly moral one. Several faults have been found in the theory and practice inculcated by the writers. Except for some centuries before and after the Christian era, monarchy has been the only form of government known in India and monarchy alone is generally envisaged by Indian writers. The result has been that the king came in practice to be almost synonymous with government and the State, though a very lofty sense of his duties and responsibilities was impressed on the king. Another defect lies in the almost total absence of discussion on the form and working of oligarchical or republican States. Besides, once the main outlines of the theory of the State were established by the first writers on polity, for about two thousand years succeeding generations of authors were content to follow in the old grooves and hardly ever made any fresh approach to the problems of government or started any rival conceptions or theories. Ancient authors were content to induce the kings and the people to support as far as possible the status quo. They thus provided for a more or less static society and did not encourage any dynamic thoughts or movements. There was no strong or assertive middle class nor was there any organized Church. Though the brāhmaṇas were a sacred class, they were not organized as a body and had to depend only on exhortations and texts to exert influence on the monarchs. It may no doubt be pointed out that similar conditions prevailed almost all the world over. Small States, constant wars and invasions were the commonest phenomena in Europe till the 15th or 16th century and no reproach should be levelled at the Indian writers alone. It cannot, however, be gainsaid that even after [[experi encing|experiencing]] the constant plundering expeditions and religious persecutions of Scythian, Hun and Moslem invaders from the [[P236]] 1st to the 11th and the following centuries the able thinkers, warriors and statesmen of India did not enlarge their limited horizon and find means to consolidate and weld together into a united block the numerous small States that were scattered all over India. They could have put forward a common idea and ideal before all the provinces and peoples of India viz. meeting the onslaught of plundering and fanatical invaders, which, if [[pro perly|properly]] handled, would have acted as a unifying force. It was to some extent only in Vijayānagara and [[Mahārāṣtra|Mahārāṣṭra]] that in medieval times means were adopted to weaken the power of the invader, to present a solid front and establish powerful Hindu kingdoms. The old writers spun the same old webs of theories that had been there for centuries, they did not formulate new theories nor did they take steps to infuse into the common people a sense of solidarity and unity as Indians and did not inculcate deep and abiding sentiments of patriotism similar to those we find in Western countries for the last two or three hundred years. In spite of such drawbacks it will have to be conceded that ancient Indian writers made substantial and independent contributions to the theory and practice of Government and that their handiwork can stand comparison with the ancient and medieval thought of most countries of the [[world,|world.]]
